chunks: Transmission line components on a PCB. The question: Describe transmission line components on a PCB.
On a circuit board, a fast signal travels along a copper trace as a wave.
The wave needs two conductors: the trace itself, and a solid reference plane under it that carries the return current. A layer of insulation (the dielectric) sits between them.
The shape of this sandwich sets the line's impedance and how fast the signal moves.
Think of a water slide with a smooth channel. The slide's width and slope decide how the water flows, and it flows the same way along its whole length.
Bumps or gaps make the water splash back. The trace plus plane is the channel. Its size sets the impedance, and any via, pad or connector along the way is a bump.
In all three the signal conductor (orange) and a return conductor (blue) with a dielectric between them form the line; thin lines indicate where the electric field goes.
Microstrip's field is partly in air so waves travel faster; stripline's all in FR-4; GCPW adds coplanar returns to tighten the field.
Reference (return) plane: the solid copper layer beside the trace. The signal's return current flows in it ("Ground plane pros and cons").
Dielectric: the insulating layer between trace and plane, often FR-4 with r about 4. 3 . L' and C': inductance and capacitance per unit length of the line.
They set the impedance and the delay ("Characteristic impedance explained").
Characteristic impedance ( Z 0 ): square root of L' over C' , the impedance a wave sees along the line.
Microstrip and stripline: a trace on an outer layer, versus a trace buried between two planes ("Choosing a board stackup").
Take a typical 50 ohms microstrip on FR-4. It has about L' equals 0. 30 nanohenries per millimeter and C' equals 0. 12 picofarads per millimeter. Then Z 0 equals square root of 0.
30 nanohenries over 0. 12 picofarads equals square root of 2500 equals 50 ohms . The delay per millimeter is square root of L'C' equals square root of 0.
30 times 10 to the -9 times 0. 12 times 10 to the -12 equals 6 picoseconds. That is the whole idea.
"A PCB transmission line is a signal trace over a reference plane with FR-4 dielectric between them.
It's microstrip if it's on an outer layer, stripline if buried between two planes.

Electrically it's a ladder of series R and L and shunt C and G per unit length; Z 0 equals square root of L' over C' and delay is square root of L'C' , about 50 ohms and 6 picoseconds/mm for a typical trace.
Along the path you also have lumped pieces, vias, pads, connectors and terminations, which are the places that cause reflections."
